Structural identification

Source: vignettes/identification.Rmd
identification.Rmd

Reduced-form innovations satisfy ut=Pεtu_t = P\varepsilon_t with PP′=ΣPP' = \Sigma. An identification scheme chooses PP. Each id_*() constructor returns a small specification object passed to the id argument of irf(), fevd() and hd(), for both varm and bvarm fits.

Implemented: id_chol(), id_longrun(), id_sign(), id_given(). Proxy/external-instrument SVAR is covered in the last section.

Cholesky (recursive)

The first variable in order is the most exogenous. Variables can be given by name.

ir1 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, nboot = 200)
ir2 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(order = c("rate", "inflation", "unemployment")),
           horizon = 12, ci = "none")
round(ir1$estimate[, , 1], 3)   # impact matrix P (response x shock)
#>               shock
#> response       inflation unemployment  rate
#>   inflation        0.308        0.000 0.000
#>   unemployment    -0.012        0.332 0.000
#>   rate             0.088       -0.268 0.715
plot(ir1)

Long-run restrictions (Blanchard-Quah)

The cumulative long-run response matrix is restricted to be lower triangular, so the second shock has no long-run effect on the first variable, and so on. Variables should be stationary growth rates or differences, and the ordering is the column order of the data. Here we use the sample series purely to show the mechanics.

ir_lr <- irf(fit, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 40, ci = "none")
ir_lr
#> <varm IRF> K = 3, horizon 0..40, id = longrun
# long-run effect: cumulative responses over a long horizon are lower triangular
ir_long <- irf(fit, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 2000, ci = "none")
round(apply(ir_long$estimate, c(1, 2), sum), 2)
#>               shock
#> response       inflation unemployment rate
#>   inflation        11.96         0.00 0.00
#>   unemployment      5.02         3.08 0.00
#>   rate             14.08         2.77 7.41

Use cumulative = "unemployment" in irf() to accumulate the response of a differenced variable into a level response.

Sign restrictions

restrictions is a K×KK \times K matrix (rows: variables, columns: shocks) with entries +1, -1 or 0 (unrestricted). A matrix is imposed over horizon periods from impact; a K×K×HK \times K \times H array gives horizon-specific restrictions. Draws use Haar-distributed rotations of the Cholesky factor (Rubio-Ramirez, Waggoner and Zha, 2010); nrot accepted rotations are kept per reduced-form draw, up to maxtry attempts. Only sign restrictions are supported; zero restrictions are not.

A stylised monetary-policy shock: the rate rises, inflation does not rise. The other two shocks are left unrestricted.

S <- matrix(0, 3, 3, dimnames = list(c("inflation", "unemployment", "rate"),
                                     c("mp", "s2", "s3")))
S["rate", "mp"] <- 1
S["inflation", "mp"] <- -1
id_sign(S, horizon = 2)   # printing an id object shows the restrictions
#> <varm_id> sign restrictions (2 at impact; 2 horizons)
#>   + positive, - negative, · unrestricted; rows = variables, cols = shocks
#>   rotations: 1 per draw, max 1000 tries
#>              mp s2 s3
#> inflation     -  ·  ·
#> unemployment  ·  ·  ·
#> rate          +  ·  ·
#> 
#> unrestricted shocks: s2, s3
ir_sign <- irf(fit, id = id_sign(S, horizon = 2, nrot = 5, maxtry = 5000),
               horizon = 16, nboot = 100)
ir_sign
#> <varm IRF> K = 3, horizon 0..16, id = sign, bands: 68%/90%
#> sign-restriction acceptance rate: 0.325

The estimate is the median across accepted rotations; for varm fits the sample-based set estimate is stored in $set_estimate. The acceptance rate is ir_sign$accept_rate. If no draw satisfies the restrictions, irf() stops with an error. Sign restrictions identify a set, so the pointwise median is not one coherent model; hd() for a varm fit uses the first accepted rotation at the point estimate.

plot(ir_sign, shocks = 1)

User-supplied impact matrix

id_given(P) takes any PP with PP′=ΣPP' = \Sigma and does not check this.

P <- t(chol(fit$Sigma))
ir_g <- irf(fit, id = id_given(P), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
all.equal(unname(ir_g$estimate[, , 1]), unname(P))
#> [1] TRUE

Using identification elsewhere 

fv <- fevd(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "none")
h  <- hd(fit, id = id_chol())

Proxy SVAR and weak-instrument-robust sets

varm_proxy() identifies one shock with an external instrument mtm_t (Mertens-Ravn, Stock-Watson): the impact vector is proportional to Γ=E[utmt]\Gamma = E[u_t m_t], normalised so the target variable moves by size. Wild-bootstrap bands are unreliable when the instrument is weak, so varm_proxy_robust() computes the Montiel Olea-Stock-Watson (2021) Anderson-Rubin-type confidence sets, valid at any instrument strength. Each set is bounded (case 1), the complement of an interval (2), empty (3) or the whole line (4); unbounded sets are reported as -Inf/Inf and empty ones as NA. proxy_fstat() reports the HAC Wald first-stage statistic F_hac that governs which case to expect.

set.seed(1)
e <- matrix(rnorm(600), 300)
y <- matrix(0, 300, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("y1", "y2")))
for (t in 2:300) y[t, ] <- 0.5 * y[t - 1, ] + c(e[t, 1] + 0.3 * e[t, 2], e[t, 2] + 0.5 * e[t, 1])
pfit <- varm(y, p = 1)
m <- e[, 1] + rnorm(300, sd = 0.5)            # relevant instrument for shock 1
proxy_fstat(pfit, m)
#>        F F_robust    F_hac 
#> 692.2304 709.8430 155.4270
rb <- varm_proxy_robust(pfit, m, horizon = 6, level = c(0.68, 0.90))
rb
#> <varm_proxy_robust> Montiel Olea-Stock-Watson sets, shock to y1 (size 1), horizon 0..6; levels 0.68, 0.9
#> HAC first-stage F = 155.4
#> 
#> normalised    bounded 
#>          2         26
round(cbind(est = rb$estimate[, "y2"], lower = rb$lower[, "y2", 2], upper = rb$upper[, "y2", 2]), 3)
#>     est  lower upper
#> 0 0.542  0.445 0.635
#> 1 0.212  0.104 0.320
#> 2 0.080 -0.011 0.172
#> 3 0.029 -0.033 0.091
#> 4 0.010 -0.028 0.047
#> 5 0.003 -0.019 0.024
#> 6 0.001 -0.011 0.012

# a pure-noise instrument: the sets become unbounded
varm_proxy_robust(pfit, rnorm(300), horizon = 3, level = 0.9)$case[, , 1]
#>   y1 y2
#> 0  0  4
#> 1  4  4
#> 2  4  4
#> 3  4  4
